Title: My Grandmother: A Memoir
Author: Fethiye Çetin
My Review:
Fethiye Cetin's "My Grandmother" is mostly the story of her grandmother who survived the Armenian genocide in 1915 because a Turk gendarme stole her from her mother and gave her to a Turkish couple. She converted to Islam and grew up as a Turk with a new name.

This memoir is a powerful story of the Armenian genocide and the consequences of it: dead and displaced family members, people hiding their identity and living in disguise and the term "leftovers of the sword".

The book has details that are depicting disguised Armenians in such an excellent way. I really loved the part about corek - convert Armenian women would bake corek for Easter and this was their secret way of keeping their identity and traditions.

"My grandmother" had little bit of everything. Despite the topic being heavy, there were moments I laughed (especially the parts that described the grandfather's eating habits), there were moments I choked and there were moments I connected.

It is always striking how different and yet similar all the stories about the genocide are. I could see parallels to my own family history. The book left me with a desire to dig deeper and to find my distant relatives who are somewhere in the world.

My Review:
The best books are those that I feel like I could have written them. Vincenzo Latronico's "Perfection" is one of them. Lightly satirical, the novel explores the emptiness and the performance culture of millennials living abroad. While many sentences were shockingly accurate and funny, one can't help but see themselves in the main characters Anna and Tom, freelance graphic designers based in Berlin but coming from somewhere else.

As a writer, what I found fascinating is that the main character was not Tom or Anna. The book didn't even have a dual protagonist. There was one main character and it was Anna and Tom as a couple, which could be generalized on an entire generation doing exactly what they did. Anna and Tom always acted together, liked and wanted the same things, except for very few situations where they disagreed.

Title: Mit arbejde
Author: Olga Ravn
My Review:
As a new mother and a writer, I gravitated towards this book and read it during those short moments I had when the baby was sleeping and I was awake.

A fragmented novel crossing genres, "Mit arbejde" tells the story of early motherhood, postpartum depression and combining this with being a writer. The book had lots of sharp observations about pregnancy, birth and the postpartum period. There were relatable experiences and also ones that were pretty foreign to me. There were thoughts that I completely disagreed with and some others that I couldn't agree more. I found Olga Ravn's take on Mary Shelley's "Frankensein" rather refreshing.

Even though this is a really important book about motherhood, I'm giving it only three stars because it severely lacked editing. I have read in an interview that originally there were 800 pages and it was cut down to 400. However, cutting another half of it would make it much sharper. The meta-text was interesting but it was getting to repetitive and too distracting. Of course, one could argue that this messiness was trying to depict the postpartum brain. But as a woman with such a brain, I would have preferred a bit more editorial work to make it easier for a postpartum brain to process.

Title: Orbital
Author: Samantha Harvey
My Review:
If books don't have plot, I can still enjoy them, if there are well-developed characters. If books don't have well-developed characters, they can still be great thanks to the great prose.

This one has nothing - no plot, no characters, no prose. Just 136 pages of pseudo-intellectual masturbation, stating the obvious that we all know about space and geography. It feels like it's written by a twelve-year-old who has just discovered that the distance between Alaska and Russia is actually pretty small and that you can't see country borders on Earth when looking from space.

The book is a failed attempt at talking about peace and claiming that we're actually not that different. It's one of those attempts when people stand for peace without really pointing to those who are responsible for peace and failing at their job. It's one of those "apolitical" novels where it doesn't take sides, nor even mentions sides, yet makes a political statement by just that - being apolitical.

Title: Scar Tissue
Author: Anthony Kiedis
My Review:
I'm not a Red Hot Chili Peppers fan, nor I became one after having heard this audiobook. Nevertheless, this was probably one of the most enjoyable artist memoirs I have ever read (if not the most enjoyable one). First of all, it is really well written and keeps the reader engaged all along. Secondly, Anthony Kiedis is rather honest about himself and respectful towards the people around him, which makes the book even more interesting. And finally, the book had a plot and an engine. Despite going through the bands musical journey, starting from the very beginnings, in the end the book is about addiction and the ways to overcome it. As a "normie" (as Kiedis himself calls those who never had any addiction), you gain a better understanding of what it means to be a drug addict. And somehow in the end you only admire the wisdom Kiedis has acquired through his addiction journey and his path to sobriety.

"Scar Tissue" is also a nice throwback to the 90s with some stories about other bands and artists like Nirvana, Pearl Jam and Sinead O'Connor. So if you're into 90s music, this book is for you.

Title: The Lost Daughter
Author: Elena Ferrante
My Review:
First watched the movie, then listened to the book. I loved the movie and I loved the book - quite a rare occurrence when both are so good.

In The Lost Daughter the narrator Leda goes on a holiday and starts observing and getting engaged with a Neapolitan family, mother and daughter in particular, which brings back memories and thoughts of her own motherhood and her own children.

Through Leda's voice we hear a taboo topic covered - a motherhood that is not as rosy, that is not a calling and is "unnatural". Leda tells the reader all the difficulties she has been through as a mother, how much of herself she had to sacrifice for her children and how much of it she wasn't willing to.

Another important issue the Elena Ferrante touches upon, though in a much more subtle way, than motherhood, is the life of a female academic compared to the male one. Both Leda and her ex-husband are academics. Somehow things had gone smoothly for the husband both before and after having children, yet it was immensely difficult for Leda to make it. We see what it means for a man and a woman to be a good scholar and a good parent at the same time. Somehow Leda could only do one: she couldn't be a successful academic and a caring mother at the same time.

I highly recommend this book (and the movie) to women who consider careers in academia, who have left academia or in general anyone who wants to explore the darker sides of motherhood.

My Review:
The first half of the book was just brilliant. As a reader, one goes into the heads of several historical figures connected to Ireland one way or the other and you learning about their dilemmas and how they navigate the world around themselves and how their actions determined history.

The second half focuses on the lives of women who appear as minor figures in the first half and follows their lives. Those women are connected through their maternal line - great-grandmother, grandmother, mother and daughter. The idea per se is brilliant, too. However, the execution was poor. And this is when the author lost me. Those characters were not as rich as the ones in the first half. It's hard to understand their motivations and the book gets quite boring in certain places.

All in all no more than 4 stars (5 for the first half and 3 for the second).

Title: The Luminaries
Author: Eleanor Catton
My Review:
With its complex structure and multiple characters, Eleanor Catton's "The Luminaries" is not just a contemporary parody of a Victorian novel, it has more to it. The mystery in itself has many layers and the motifs of the characters are multi-dimensional. If one simplifies the plot, it can be categorized as trash. But what makes "The Luminaries" a true work of art is the amount of effort the author has put in creating it.

There are 12 astral characters and 7 planetary ones. Most of the story is told from the point of view of the astral characters, yet it is about the planetary characters. The latter seem distant, the reader doesn't get into their heads, yet they are the main drivers of the book, their interactions are what makes the plot progress.

Structurally, the book starts slow with a rather long setup and gradually gets faster, in the end giving the reader the sense of being short of breath.

The astrology in the book is not just there, it also determines the characters and the events described in each chapter, showing the meticulous work the author has put into it.

Some events in the book remain unexplained but actually those are meant for the most attentive to be rewarded for noticing those small details.

All in all, "The Luminaries" brought back the joy of reading as a child, when I wouldn't want to put down a book and I'd stick to the page until the very last moment of it. Due its complexity, it also deserves a reread to notice all the little details and to fully understand the plot.

Title: Les Années
Author: Annie Ernaux
My Review:
This was absolutely one of the best books I've ever read.

A book where I had to stop at every sentence, re-read, sometimes aloud, sometimes in translation, share it with friends.

A book, which despite being about France and which often had references I didn't get, made me feel at home.

A book that I'm definitely going to read again at some point in the future.

In The Years, Annie Ernaux is telling her own life story in post-WWII France until the early 21st century interwoven with history. Through the passing years we see the change in the little girl growing into a woman and then ageing and we see all the changes France and the world goes through. We see the political and cultural references. We see the political and personal intertwined and inseparable. And things happening today start making more sense.

This is not an autobiography or a memoire. It's telling history in a personal way.

This is a must-read for leftists, for feminists and for those who are interested in the why and the how we got where we are today.

Title: Seven Empty Houses
Author: Samanta Schweblin
My Review:
With Seven Empty Houses I completed reading everything Samanta Schweblin has ever published in English. In that sense there were no surprises: her classic style of keeping the reader hooked, touching uncomfortable topics, disturbing the reader. Some of the short stories were better than the others.

But what I found interesting was the theme of parenthood is all over Schweblin's work: Fever Dream, some of the short stories in Mouthful of Birds (including the title one), some aspects of Little Eyes and now Seven Empty Houses. It's amazing how she keeps coming back to the same topic from different angles, different perspectives (parent, child, spouse) and different ages (the eight-year-old narrator in The Unlucky Man and the old woman in Breath from the Depths).

Seven Empty Houses wouldn't be a classic Samanta Schweblin book, if parenting was the only topic she touched. There was also social inequality, getting old and having a neurodegenerative disease, man-woman relationships, prejudices, etc.

If you have read Schweblin before and want more, I highly recommend reading Seven Empty Houses. If you haven't, start with Fever Dream and then read the rest.

Title: All the Light We Cannot See
Author: Anthony Doerr
My Review:
A recipe for writing an American bestseller:

1. Pick a traumatic topic (war always works, WWII is the best)
2. Make orphan kids as your main characters (bonus points, if one of them has a disability, such as blindness)
3. Put an evil villain
4. Make the evil villain chase the girl and the boy save the girl (bonus points, if the girl is saved and the boy dies)
5. Add elements of fantasy
6. Make the structure non-linear (a non-regular reader will never find out this has been done a lot)
7. Turn up the emotions. The more, the merrier. Clichés are welcome.
8. Do not dare to touch any hard topics, such as politics. Do not make the book about something important
9. Spice up with some rapist Russians

"All the Light We Cannot See" is following this recipe to perfection. In fact, doing it so well that it even managed to get a Pulitzer prize.

This is a book meant for people who have never experienced war and read books about war to shed a tear or two and move on.

Title: Slaughterhouse-Five
Author: Kurt Vonnegut Jr.
My Review:
I've been in Dresden. I know there was bombing during WWII and that it was so massive that even in 2006 they still had not finished the reconstruction. Nevertheless, it seemed abstract and distant until I read Vonnegut's "Slaughterhouse-Five".

The novel follows Billy Pilgrim, a WWII veteran and a former POW, while he travels through time and space. We see PTSD inside out, from the perspective of the person who has it. We also learn what the Dresden bombing was all out: nobody was supposed to survive. And then we learn the level of devastation and the destruction and it feels so close that under no circumstances you don't want to witness any other war.

Title: The Goldfinch
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review:
Donna Tartt's "The Goldfinch" is probably one of the most overrated books I have ever read.

Spanning across 770 pages with irrelavant details, messy and (I daresay) bad writing, it feels more like somebody's first draft than a Pulitzer-prize winning novel.

Most characters were rather unlikeable, others were flat. The plot had many holes and inconsistencies (has anyone ever edited this book?). And it dragged on and on forever like a never-ending nightmare full of pseudo-intellectual musings.

While the first third felt like a pretentious, somebody's overly ambitious attempt to impress the reader with descriptions of New York, starting from Las Vegas and onwards it felt like a bad Hollywood action movie, interrupted with discussions about Dostoyevsky and art. In fact, the book was so American that it seemed the author couldn't live without pulling out a gun and of all the places in the most unlikely one - in Amsterdam.

All in all a mediocre, poorly written brick that doesn't deserve the praise it has received so far. And please, don't compare "The Goldfinch" to anything Dickens has written.

Title: Zabelle
Author: Nancy Kricorian
My Review:
3.5 stars
Nancy Kricorian's "Zabelle" is the story of the Armenian Genocide survivor Zabelle who moves to the US for an arranged marriage, has kids and grandchildren who grow up as Americans.

This novel covers topics like the Armenian Genocide, motherhood and identity of Armenian Americans. Apart for being a yet another valuable and important novel that covers the atrocities our people were forced to go through in the early 20th century, it is also a source of information for those of us who don't know much about Armenian Americans and their identity struggles. Nancy Kricorian not only managed to accurately portray the fact that second generation Armenians drift away from their roots but also she dissected the entire process and showed why those things happened.

What I missed in the later parts of the novel (that is, after Zabelle fell off the stairs) was a bit of drama and tension. The topics were there. But they were briefly covered and skipped and thus making the novel rather monotonous (hence 3.5 stars).

In any case, I recommend reading this book to those who want to learn more about the diasporan identity.

Title: Against White Feminism: Notes on Disruption
Author: Rafia Zakaria
My Review:
This book came to my attention when I, as an Armenian feminist, was looking into ways of combining Armenianness and feminism - two concepts that have been traditionally seen as contradictory.

While Rafia Zakaria says nothing about women of Armenia, she definitely discusses other non-white women, their struggles and feminism, and how white feminists often misunderstand them or even present themselves as "the white saviour". It is especially valuable that Zakaria goes throughout history and digs the feminist movements in the West, putting them into the context of non-white women's struggle.

Towards the end of the book there is a call for unity and for creating a united feminist agenda. "We must unite behind political claims," she writes, "and perhaps the most important of those claims is that the dominance of capitalism is bad for all women, even white women."

This was definitely a great starting point on my journey of talking about Armenian feminism, which has so far been only described from a white feminist's perspective.

My Review:
Naoise Dolan is often compared to Sally Rooney, thus being shadowed by her fame, coming as the "second". What's not to compare? Both Irish women of the same generation writing roughly about the same things.
But Naoise Dolan is different. Better.
"Exciting Times" is set in Honk Kong where the young Irish woman Ava is trying to build her life and is caught in a love triangle between a man and a woman. The character work is extremely good. Despite the many flaws the main character has, one grows to like her. There is also lots of humour.

Title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)
Author: J.K. Rowling
My Review:
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire is undoubtedly the most political one of all the Harry Potter books so far, and had the potential of being the best one. However, the book is a complete mess and full of lazy writing.

The story is full of soap and goes to nowhere. Lots of weird things are happening and no clues are given along the way. Some obvious red herrings are thrown at the reader and that's it. Lots of unnecessary details and boring subplots. Only in the end everything is explained in three long monologues. One has the impression that the author had written some 500 pages before she realised things need explanation and instead of building it up, she just threw it in the end. The S.P.E.W. subplot was entirely abandoned and led to nowhere.

The book certainly lacked heavy editing and probably it wasn't necessary, considering J.K. Rowling's fame. Had this been the first Harry Potter book, she wouldn't be able to get away with this. And it's kind of sad because this could have easily been a brilliant book with some proper editing.

Title: Childhood (The Copenhagen Trilogy, #1)
Author: Tove Ditlevsen
My Review:
Tove Ditlevsen's "Childhood" tells the story of the author's childhood in the then working class Vesterbro in Copenhagen. We follow Tove's character from being a child and making her first attempts to write poems to the moment of her confirmation.

Written in a beautiful language and the specific Tove Ditlevsen style humor, the book gives the reader an idea not only about what was going on in the young Tove's head but also the social-democratic movement, the lives of working class families and family structures in Vesterbro.

Living in Vesterbro myself, close to Hedebygade 30A, I found the book fascinating. Like the fictionalized version of this book "Barndommens gade", "Childhood" also drew me closer to my surroundings in Vesterbro. In the book, I could recognize every little street, also the one where I live and I could see how the times have changed certain aspects of Vesterbro but some others remain the same.

A highly recommended read for those interested in Danish literature, culture and history but especially for those who live in Vesterbro.

Perhaps though this would be a good young adult read for those who like the genre.

Title: De ansatte
Author: Olga Ravn
My Review:
Olga Ravn's "The Employees" is a workplace Sci-Fi novel and consists of statements (in random order?) written by employees of a spaceship. With lack of plot and strong characters, it is a tough book to go through, despite its small size. It is, however, one of those books one considers revisiting.

The topics covered in the book include the capitalistic work structure (is it failing?) and, more importantly, what it means to be human. Certain characters are dehumanizing others, while others are scared of seeming human. In fact, not all characters are human, some are just "humanoids".

The author gives clues to the reader to find connections between the statements. One reader on their own cannot do it reading it only once. This is why it's a great book to discuss in a book club to put together bits and pieces and to make sense of what the book is actually about.

Title: Beautiful World, Where Are You
Author: Sally Rooney
My Review:
3.5 stars

Sally Rooney's previous two books had a huge effect on me. So naturally I had been waiting for this book since 2018. But I'm disappointed.

"Beautiful World, Where Are You" tells the story of two young women in their late twenties, trying to figure their lives out. Alice is an acclaimed writer, her best friend Eileen works for a literary magazine. Alice is dating Felix. Eileen is figuring out her relationship with her childhood friend Simon.

The book can be summarized in one sentence: lots of sex, interrupted with emails, then pages with no paragraphs.

Rooney's third book is not extremely different from the previous two. Alice's and Eileen's relationship is "Conversations with Friends" and Eileen's and Simon's relationship is "Normal People." At first glance, what is there not to like?

Unlike the characters from the previous two books, those ones are extremely annoying and one doesn't feel sympathy for them, nor finds them relatable. But these characters are meant to be relatable with all their millennial dating lifestyle and the kind of intimate conversations they have.

It seems that Rooney has figured out what has worked previously and turned the level up: more sex, way too much, more unspoken stuff and more technology. Other than the emails there is a lot of messaging, a lot of description of what is going on on the characters' phone screens. Rooney seems to have figured out though that the longs electronic communication in "Conversations with Friends" was too much, so she kept the emails short and to the point, to some extent.

The abrupt change of styles from chapter to chapter gave the impression that most of the book had been written in workshops. I couldn't help but think that certain chapters were born as a result of writing exercises and haven't been polished to fit the whole picture.

The book could have two endings. I have a feeling that Sally Rooney's original ending was two chapters before the book actually ended and someone had advised her to add some stuff about the pandemic and give it some kind of a happy ending or something. It absolutely didn't work. I would have much preferred the real Rooneyesque open to interpretation ending.

As I really like Sally Rooney as a writer, I really hope her next book will be better and perhaps exploring new territories that she hasn't explored so far.

My Review: One of Hemingway's minor novels. The book is focused on class and poverty. In To Have and Have Not he is clearly exploring the different ways a novel can be written. One encounters a lot of stream of consciousness, which is quite unusual for Hemingway's writing. What he tries out in this novel he ultimately perfects in For Whom the Bell Tolls.

Title: Voices of the Lost
Author: Hoda Barakat
My Review:
The book is set as series of letters. The author of each letter is the unintended reader of the previous one and is inspired to write their own. Although the letters are authored by people with different backgrounds, age and gender, they are all united by one thing: they are all the lost, in a foreign country, with no sense of a homeland, as their homeland is torn apart by a civil war. Through the letters we learn the most intimate secrets of their authors, we learn about their desperation and their humble wishes of living a decent human life.

In the second part of the novel we encounter "the other viewpoint" of affairs, where the addressees of the letters tell their version of the story. Whose side are you going to take? Who are you going to believe?

In the final part we encounter the postman who can no longer deliver letters because the addressees and the addresses are not there anymore.

Hoda Bakarat's "Voices of the Lost" is a masterful depiction of war trauma, of the irreversible changes it makes in people and of the ignorance of the rest of the world. Highly recommended, if you want to learn what a person goes through when their country is in war.

Title: The Beekeeper of Aleppo
Author: Christy Lefteri
My Review:
This book is a typical example of a Western writer monetizing on other people's sufferings and the Western reader reading it and feeling content that they are "informed" of other people's sufferings, closing the book and going about their daily lives or in some cases "getting involved". The unusually and undeservingly high Goodreads rating is a proof of that.

"The Beekeeper of Aleppo" is the story of a Syrian beekeeper Nuri and his wife, escaping Syria to find refuge in the UK. The book attempts (yes, only attempts!) covering the hardships a refugees go through to reach a safe haven.

What I terribly missed in this book was the political background. I know the Syria issue is a rather complex one and a novel writer cannot disentangle this complexity. But the way this novel ended up being is that out of nowhere some bad guys came to Syria and started bombing and killing people. I imagine, this is what is expected of the Western reader to know about the issue. It is expected not to ask difficult questions, such as what was the role of their own governments in creating the mess Syria is in? It is expected to "get involved" (i.e. white saviour type of volunteering and helping out the refugees and feeling good about themselves, perhaps adding this to their CVs) but not hold their own governments accountable.

The plot is non-linear and this is what makes the book even worse than it could actually be. No proper character work, no good plot, no good writing. In fact, this was one of those books that would largely benefit from a classic linear plot, which would make it less boring and would get the reader hooked to find out the answer to the question whether the characters finally made it to the UK.

The story felt like an averaged out refugee story and not the story of a particular couple. The only emotion the novel generated in me was anger, anger towards the writer, towards the readers who have loved this book, towards all those who read books on other people's sufferings and feel it's all they need to do to change the world. And I guess this is exactly what their governments want them to do. So congratulations, this book was a success.

Title: The Eighth Life
Author: Nino Haratischwili
Additional Authors: Charlotte Collins, Ruth   Martin, Nino Haratischvili
My Review:
Nino Haratischwili's The Eighth Life is a family saga that spans over a hundred years and through the story of the family tells the Georgian history of 20th century. The story starts with the independence of Georgia in early 20th century, goes to the October revolution and Sovietisation of Georgia, all the different periods of the Soviet Union, the fall of the Soviet Union and the independence of Georgia once again until the Rose Revolution and the disappointment from it.

The author doesn't spare the reader and goes through the horrors of each and every period, showing the reality as it is, with the way it affects the entire nation and the main characters in the story.
The novel is primarily focused on female characters with their rich personalities and their dreams, their hopes and their peculiarities. The male characters are often poorly developed and dull, with the exception of Kostya, who was trying to play the role of the patriarch of the family and controlling the lives of the others, using all the power he had. But it didn't quite work out, as the women broke free, each one in their own way.

The narrator - Nitsa - is Kostya's granddaughter and, interestingly, the one most like him, who was trying to control the world around her and the story she has written for her niece Brilka is the ultimate attempt at controlling lives around her.

The novel is not only the history of Georgia but also a story of shattered dreams, of time passing and not letting people become who they actually wanted to become, yet there is slight hope, hope for Brilka, whose life might turn out differently from those of others in her family.

As an Armenian, this was a great read for me. I learned a great deal about our neighbouring country, about our similarities and differences, about our common history and about how they see us.

The book was a bit soapy and slightly boring in some places but overall I highly recommend it for those who want to learn more not only about Georgia but also the Soviet Union and the pre- and post-Soviet era in general.

Title: Այն եզդի կնոջ ճամպրուկը
Author: Tereza  Amryan
My Review:
Թերեզա Ամրյանի «Այդ եզդի կնոջ ճանպրուկը» կարդալիս շարունակ մի հարց էի տալիս ինքս ինձ. ինչու՞ մենք եզդիների մասին այսքան քիչ բան գիտենք։ Ամեն դեպքում, այս գրքով Թերեզա Ամրյանը կարծես բացը լրացրել է ինչ-որ չափով. իր ընտանիքի պատմությունը համադրելով եզդիների մասին ակադեմիական գիտելիքներով՝ Թերեզա Ամրյանն ընթերցողին է ներկայացնում եզդիների մշակութային առանձահատկություններն ու պատմության կարևոր կետերը։ Ու դա անում է սիրով ու հպարտությամբ, գրքի էջերից զգացվում է սեփական ժողովրդի նկատմամբ անմնացորդ սերը։ Հեղինակը, խորությամբ հասկանալով իր ժողովրդի ավանդույթները, նաև մատնացույց է անում, թե որտեղ դրանք պետք է փոխվեն (օրինակ՝ կանանց կրթություն ստանալու հարցը)։

Հեղինակն անդրադառնում է նաև արևմուտքի կեղծավորությանը, ու թե ինչպես քսանմեկերորդ դարում եզդի ժողովրդի ցեղասպանություն թույլ տվեցին բոլորի աչքի առաջ. մի բան, որ հազվադեպ էր արևմտյան լրատվամիջոցներ մտնում։

Գիրքն ընդհանուր առմամբ գրված է բարի, միամիտ տոնով։ Որպես ընթերցող հեղինակի սերը սեփական ժողովրդի նկատմամբ փոխանցվում է նաև քեզ։ Ավելի լավ ես հասկանում եզդիներին, ավելի շատ գնահատում Հայաստանի Հանրապետության գոյության փաստը, որովհետև այս պետությունը ոչ միայն հայ, այլև եզդի ժողովրդի անվտանգության երաշխիքն է։

Գրքի լեզուն մի քիչ կաշկանդված էր, ու լավ խմբագրումից հաստատ կշահեր։ Ամեն դեպքում, եթե ուզում եք մեզ հարազատ եզդի ժողովրդի մասին ավելին իմանալ, անպայման կարդացեք այս գիրքը. սա անձնականի ու գիտականի հրաշալի համադրություն է։

Title: BOB
Author: Helle Helle
My Review:
Bob and his girlfriend (they first appear in Helle Helle's "de") move to Copenhagen, more specifically to Vanløse. From there on we follow Bob, as he finds a job in a hotel and wanders around and encounters people and takes a train out of the city.

Although the novel has a first narrator who is Bob's girlfriend, the story is told as an omnipotent narrator would. We learn that despite living with his girlfriend, Bob is often alone in the evenings and doesn't rush to get home. The girlfriend is absent from her relationship, she just tells the story as a matter of fact, like she is not part of Bob's life.

Helle Helle's each new book is a treat and "Bob" isn't an exception. The elegance of her language, the beauty of each sentence and the sympathy towards the main character are inspiring and make one want to write their own story. I often read Helle Helle to overcome writer's block and "Bob" was the best remedy I could find this time around.

Title: The Memory Police
Author: Yōko Ogawa
My Review:
On an unnamed island things disappear. Hats, fruit, photographs, etc. People are supposed to forget about these concepts after their disappearance and if they don't, the memory police comes after them.

The setup is brilliant, it prepares the reader for a dystopian sci-fi novel that could have many parallels with our current societies. The execution, however, is fairly poor. The book drags on and on, describing disappearances, memory police visits, etc. But there are too many plot holes, too many Checkov's guns that don't shoot and the character work is poor. I would forgive the latter, if it had a great plot. But the lack of plot and lack of character make the second half of the book completely boring. Also, the ending doesn't make sense at all. It feels lazy and meaningless.

My Review:
Վեպի գլխավոր իրադարձությունները տեղի են ունենում Փարիզի մի ծննդատան սպասասրահում։ Այստեղ աղքատ կանայք, որոնք ինչ-ինչ պատճառներով չեն կարող իրենց երեխաներին կրծքով կերակրել, հավաքվում են կաթ ստանալու։ Նրանցից է նաև Էվան՝ հրեա մի կին, որ ամուսնացել է ֆրանսիացի Անտրէի հետ ու տեղափոխվել Ֆրանսիա։

Սպասման սրահն այն վայրն է, որտեղ աղքատները հանդիպում են նախկին աղքատներին. հիվանդապահուհիները, թեև նույն ստորին դասակարգից են, աշխատանքի են տեղավորվել ծննդատանը, հետևաբար իրենց ապրուստի հարցը լուծել են, մինչ կաթ ստացող կանայք ծայրահեղ աղքատ են, բացարձակապես ոչ մի կոպեկ չունեն գպանում։ Հիվանդապահուհիների մեջ սաստիկ չարություն կա այցելու կանանց նկատմամբ։ Նրանց ստորացնում են, ծաղրում, ըստ իրենց քմահաճույքի անգամ զրկում կաթից։

Էդպես կաթից զրկում են նաև Էվային։ Էվան ու Անտրէն այնքան աղքատ են, որ ամիսներով պարտքեր ունեն կուտակած, իրենք էլ օրերով ոչինչ չեն ուտում, բայց երեխային կերակրելը հրատապ է։ Սակայն մի վեճի ժամանակ հիվանդապահուհին Էվային էլ է զրկում կաթից, ու ընտանիքով հայտնվում են լրիվ անելանելի դրության մեջ։ Ընտանիքի բարեկամ Սատարօֆը միջնորդում է, բժիշկ Բրացը հիվանդապահուհիների վրա ճնշում գործադրի, ու Էվային կաթ տան։

Ու Էվան սպասման սրահում երկարուձիգ ժամեր է անցկացնում՝ սպասելով Բրացին։ Էվան նաև թեթևակի սիրահարվել է նրան, փրկության է սպասում։ Բայց Բրացը, թեև սիրալիր է Էվայի նկատմամբ, լինելով այլ դասակարգից, վերևից է նայում աղքատներին. «Ա՜Հ անանկ տգիտութիւն մը, յամառութիւն մը կայ այդ ստորին դասակարգին մէջ որ հակառակ բոլոր բարի կամեցողութեան բան մը ընել կարելի չէ»։

Սպասման սրահը նաև այն վայրն է, որտեղ աղքատների ժամանակը չի գնահատվում, ու կարելի է նրանց սպասեցնել այնքան, որքան ուզենան։ Վերջում, երբ Անտրէն հիվանդանոց է ընկնում, Էվան ու Սատարօֆը գնում են տեսակցության ու ժամերով սպասում են սպասասրահում, մինչ բժիշկները կճաշեն, կհանգստանան ու կբարեհաճեն իրենցով զբաղվել։

Ընդհանուր առմամբ, «Սպասման սրահին մէջ» վեպով Զապէլ Եսայեանը ցույց է տալիս, թե աղքատները որքան մենակ են իրենց խնդիրներով, ու դրանց որքան անհաղորդ են մնացածները՝ լինեն նրանք նախկին աղքատներ, թե առավել բարեկեցիկ կյանք ունեցողներ։

My Review:
Set in a fictional location called Maran (which is obviously a remote Armenian village), the novel tells the story of the aged villagers. Full of magic realism and Armenian culture and beliefs, the book is accurately capturing Armenian rural life.

While the story is well-written and easy to follow, its content is mostly feel-good stuff and possibly meant for young adults.

Title: Biler og dyr
Author: Helle Helle
My Review:
After having read several of Helle Helle's novels, I was sure she was more of a short story writer. Indeed, "Biler og dyr", being a short story collection, shows Helle Helle's writing skills in a stronger light. With minimalistic language and well-crafted dialogues Helle Helle is exploring the lives of the most ordinary people with their ordinary mundane problems. These characters would normally not be interesting enough for writers to write about but Helle Helle's mastery is finding the fascinating aspects of being human and telling their stories, translating their emotions to words, which are not always direct translations.

As a writer myself, I find Helle Helle one of those few writers that inspire me a lot. The biggest lesson learnt from her stories: tell as much as you can with as few words as possible.

My Review: Էս գիրքը, ինչպես ժամանակակից հայ գրականության շատ գրքեր, ունի մի բավական լուրջ թերություն. թեեւ լեզվի հետ հրաշալի էքսպերիմետներ են կատարվում, չունի սյուժե, չունի կերպարներ։ Անգամ պոեզիա չի։ Պարզապես սիրուն նախադասությունների հավաքածու։

Title: Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead
Author: Olga Tokarczuk
My Review:
3.5 stars
The story is told from the perspective of an old woman Janina living in a Polish village bordering Czech Republic. The novel is a murder mystery but written in an extremely boring way that more than once I was considering leaving the book.

The character work of Janina was brilliant though: vegan, animal lover, translating Blake and slightly crazy. But there was almost no plot, just someone was murdered every once in a while. Even those murders as plot points failed to grab the reader's attention and make you want to learn more. However, as a reader, when you close the final page, you somehow feel sympathy for the murderer, which is why the novel is probably more successful than not because it achieves something really important that gets you to question the reality you live in.

The novel is going into topics like animal rights, loneliness and usefulness for the society. Are people like Janina and her friends useful for the society? Do humans have the right to carelessly murder animals?

Finally, I don't rule out that the boringness of the book was also because of the translation. Maybe there was strong language work that was completely missed in the translation.

Title: Nowhere, a Story of Exile
Author: Anna Astvatsaturian Turcotte
My Review:
The book is a memoir of a young Armenian girl growing up in Baku, Azerbaijan. As the violence against Armenians rises in Azerbaijan, her family has no other choice but fleeing Baku and trying to build a home in Yerevan, Armenia. But the young Anna doesn't feel home in Yerevan either. Eventually the family moves to the US.

"Nowhere, a Story of Exile" above all is an important documentation of ethnic cleansing of Armenians in Azerbaijan and of the Armenian refugees that the world knows nothing about. Told from a perspective of a little girl and thus being largely uncensored, the book describes the horrors Armenians in Azerbaijan had to go through. It also raises the question of Armenian identity. What does it mean to be Armenian? Is it speaking Armenian? If so, then why were Azeris after Armenians who didn't speak Armenian? Is it the last name ending in -ian? If so, why didn't the Astvatsaturovs feel safe in Baku?

As an Armenian, this is a question that has been bothering me a lot throughout my lifetime and "Nowhere, a Story of Exile" gave me the answer: you're Armenian, if your life is in danger in Azerbaijan.

I highly recommend this book to all Armenians, especially those living in Armenia both to learn more about the Armenians from Baku and also to see the best and the worst side of us as a nation. I recommend to those who are interested in the Artsakh (Nagorno Karabakh) issue and the consequences it had for Armenians. In the end, I recommend this to everyone who has ever criticized a refugee, no matter where they are from.

Title: Swing Time
Author: Zadie Smith
My Review:
The book starts being about two brown girls growing up in London together and then shifts to something else. The first hundred pages or so were compelling and really well written but that was about it. The book lost me when the first time shift happened (we jump from the two girls being in their pre-teens to being in their early twenties). This is where Aimee - an Australian pop star is introduced (reminding of Kylie Minogue?) and the narrator becomes her personal assistant.

Zadie Smith, no doubt, is a skilled writer and she is also a great storyteller. However, structurally the novel suffered a lot. The non-linear structure was absolutely not justified. In fact, it was often frustrating. Many of the side stories and secondary characters seemed to have no purpose and nothing to do with the main story. In fact, it is quite difficult to tell what exactly the main story was. Was it the unnamed character's friendship with Tracey? If so, why spend so much time with Aimee and her life in West Africa. Is the book about fame and what it does to people? If so, why dig so much into the friendship? Is it about mother-daughter relationship (in fact, the stronger aspect of the novel)?

The novel had couple of loose ends: why were the half-siblings introduced, if they had nothing to do with the story? When, why and how did the father die? What was so crazy about Tracey's letter that led the two of them not talking to each other? In fact, the build-up to that moment was exaggerated. One was expecting something gravely serious and not what appeared in the letter.

In "Swing Time" Zadie Smith scratches the surface of many different topics such as race, identity, friendship, class, mother-daughter relationship, poverty tourism, etc. without never really going deeper into any of those. All of them really important and interesting, yet bastardized in this kind of writing.

But what upset me the most was the author confused an Iranian character, turning him into an Arab. This kind of carelessness is completely unacceptable to me, especially in a book that is trying to talk about delicate subjects like race and identity.

Title: Beloved
Author: Toni Morrison
My Review:
If there is one book in the world every white person should read to understand American racism, slavery and what black people have been through, it is Toni Morrison's "Beloved."

With elements of horror and magic realism Toni Morrison is telling us about slavery, freedom, the emotional impact slavery has on black people, their fears and their love. The book takes us to the roots of racism and how everything started and continued. There is no other book I have previously read that tells American history so well. No other American book I've read has so many topics to discuss.

Title: Barndommens gade
Author: Tove Ditlevsen
My Review:
First of all, this is one of the best pieces of Danish literature I have ever read. Now let's move ahead.

"Barndommens gade" ("Childhood Street") is a novel set in 30s Copenhagen. The main character is Esther in her teens. She is growing up in a working class family and lives on Hedebygade.

The entire story is told from Esther's perspective. At times it's funny, at times it's sad. All the way it's brilliantly written. Ditlevsen has this unique ability of getting into the mind of a teenager and telling the story entirely from her perspective.

As a reader you learn a lot about the 30s Copenhagen, the struggles of the working class, the culture and politics. As a foreigner in Copenhagen, I can't recommend this book enough to those who want to learn more about Denmark and Copenhagen. "Barndommens gade" truly shows the roots of all the social and cultural constructs that make Denmark what it is today. A must read.

Title: Lost Children Archive
Author: Valeria Luiselli
My Review:
Valeria Luiselli's "Lost Children Archive" is a documentation of how a family of four is falling apart, while on a road trip in the US. But most importantly, it is also about the undocumented children that cross the US border, hoping for a better life. These two journeys intertwine at some point.

Valeria Luiselli is the kind of author that I really like following and checking all her new books. And I'm amazed how her writing gets better with every new book. In "Lost Children Archive" her writing is taken to the next level and it's extremely enjoyable reading the female narrator's story, going through her personal drama and also covering the political - the lost children.

There is a lot of focus on sound. The entire book has lots of sound effects - songs, audio books, nature sounds, voices, echoes. Apart from the central topic, the sound approach is one of the core strengths of the novel. You read it but you also hear lots of sound, and Luiselli has done it masterfully.

There are many references to other literary works and the book feels like a reward for those readers who have previously read these other works because the references are not there just for being there but they are an integral part of the story. For instance, having read Roberto Bolaño's "2666" helps the reader understand what the refugee children may be escaping from.

As ambitious as Luiselli's attempts may be, at times she's failing to deliver what she is aiming for. Specifically, the book within the book is really not working, or the Bolaño-style 10+ pages long sentences is really difficult to get through. However, she should be praised for the bravery.

Valeria Luiselli is certainly a rising star in contemporary literature, an author whose every book I look forward to and whose creative journey is fascinating to follow.

Title: Every Fire You Tend
Author: Sema Kaygusuz
My Review:
"Every Fire You Tend" is about trauma. The author integrates her grandmother's stories of the Zaza-speaking Alevi Kurds massacres in Dersim, Turkey in 1937-38 with her own experience of intergenerational trauma, making it into a poetic narrative, intertwined with mythology. The second person character is some sort of mix of the narratore and the grandmother Bese - a survivor of the massacres. There is nothing graphic and very little information explicitly mentioning what has happened in Dersim. But as a reader you get it. You get it because you had your own great-grandmother telling similar stories. You get it because it is written in the language of trauma and those of us who carry an intergenerational trauma, don't need every word explained. As the author herself puts it, the book is written in the language of figs.

Highly recommended to Armenian readers.

Title: The Blind Assassin
Author: Margaret Atwood
My Review:
If you really want to enjoy Margaret Atwood's "The Blind Assasin", you need to be prepared to spend time on it. This is not the kind of the novel that you sit down and read and then you're done. "The Blind Assassin" is rather complex. It has a story within a story within a story. But this is not the only thing that makes it rather cognitively demanding when reading it.

The book starts with the narrator's sister (Laura Chase) dying in a car crash, most probably a suicide. The rest of the novel evolves around the narrator's and her sister's relationship - all the way back to childhood, growing up in a small town, the two world wars and the events leading to Laura's death. But then the story also has a novel embedded in it, written by Laura Chase. In this novel there is yet another story being told, this time about a blind assassin. And of course, in the end there is a giant plot twist or rather couple of them.

What Margaret Atwood does so brilliantly in this novel is rewarding the attentive reader way before reaching the end. If you're an attentive reader and if you go back and re-read some of the early pages in the book, there are things that you figure out much earlier than they are explicitly mentioned in the book. And thus the plot twist is not a plot twist anymore but something the author had told you early on.

Oh, also the blind assassin is probably not (only) the character in the story in the novel within the novel. Figuratively speaking, some other character in the book could also be the blind assassin but I'm leaving that for the reader to figure out.

Author: Emmanuel Carrère

Title: P/F
Author: Aram Pachyan
My Review:
Պաչյանի P/F-ն Երևանում մեծացած ու Երևանը կարոտածիս համար հենց էն էր, ինչ պետք էր կարդալ էս իրավիճակում։ Գիրքը Երևանն է որ կա՝ հատվածավորված, փոփոխական, բազմաշերտ, սրճարաններով, փողոցներով, ցեխոտ ձյունով, այլևս գոյություն չունեցող Գետառով ու միայնությամբ։ Պաչյանն ընթերցողին Երևանով զբոսանքի է տանում, անցկացնում էնպիսի ծակուծուկերով, որոնցով միայն Երևանը ոտքից գլուխ ճանաչող, տարիներով քաղաքը ոտքի տակ տված, բոլոր սրճարանները հերթով այցելած մեկը կիմանա։ Հերոսի հետ անցնում ես էդ բոլոր տեղերով ու հերթով կարոտդ առնում։

Ամենից շատ Պաչյանի լեզուն եմ սիրում։ P/F-ն էլ բացառություն չէ, էստեղ էլ հայերենն էնպիսի վարպետությամբ է օգտագործում, որ բոլոր նորարարություններն ականջդ շոյում են, ուզում ես նորից ու նորից կարդալ, երբեմն նաև բարձրաձայն, որ լսես լեզուն։ Պաչյանի հայերենը շնչում է, կենդանի է, միևնույն ժամանակ՝ յուրօրինակ ու հաճելի, ինչը ժամանակակից հայ գրականության մեջ բացառիկ համադրություն է։

Title: The Caucasian Chalk Circle
Author: Bertolt Brecht
My Review:
Why do I not read plays so often?

Brecht's Caucasian Chalk Circle is set in Georgia (the reason why I picked up the book - the only one in the entire bookstore that was remotely related to "my part of the world) where two mothers - a rich one and a poor one - claim ownership of a child. Unlike Solomon's story though, "Caucasian Chalk Circle" provides a new definition of "real motherhood", which is not necessarily biology.

The story is told by Singer, thus making the play very musical, you can almost hear it while reading it. Structurally, it's brilliant, I assume that is the case with all classic plays. Ideologically, it's leftist in a layered and nuanced way. I recommend reading this to those of you who are looking for brilliant plays to read. It's pure enjoyment.

Title: Thinking In Pictures: and Other Reports from My Life with Autism
Author: Temple Grandin
My Review:
A great read, if you want to understand autism beyond research articles. Temple Grandin has done an excellent work of combining the personal and the scientific. Through bringing in scientific findings into her own experience, Grandin gives the reader the opportunity to see what it feels like to have an autistic brain.

The book could be edited a bit because it had lots of repetitions but all in all it was worth the read.

Title: Who Put This Song On?
Author: Morgan  Parker
My Review:
The reason why I read "Who Put This Song On?" was, well, I liked the title and I bought the book. It's the story of a teenage black girl who struggles to fit in, being not black enough among black people and not white enough among white people. The book challenges the stereotypical views of what it means to be black. It also shows the daily racism black people face in the US. The main character - Morgan - is brave and she fights that racism in every way she can. The novel also goes to some dark places like teenage depression, at the same time shows the value of great friendships.

The most surprising thing about the book was how relatable it was. Set in the US, with American cultural references, a black girl in a white environment having troubles to fit it, it still reminds me of my own childhood in Armenia, where I was having struggles to fit in because of the way I dressed and the music I listened to. If you had similar experiences, I highly recommend reading the book. But also, read it, if you're curious about depression in teenagers or racism in the US or simply just want to read a good book.

Title: Fakta om Finland
Author: Erlend Loe
My Review:
Erlend Loe's "Fakta om Finland" ("Facts about Finland") is yet another example of how reading only in English limits your access to many wonderful literary works. "Fakta om Finland" has never been translated to English (and probably never will). I have read the book in Norwegian and it was quite a struggle for someone like me - a non-native speaker of Danish. But the reward was so great that it was worth it.

An unnamed narrator who is also a graphic designer is making a brochure to advertise Finland in Norway. For someone who has lived in the Nordic countries, this alone is already pretty funny. But there is more to the book.

"Fakta om Finland" has that same tone that I have first encountered in Loe's "Naive. Super". The narrator has the same type of naivete that is quite funny at many places and the same type of loneliness and is going through a similar existential crisis. In this book, however, Loe has perfected his writing style and his language.

In the book there are numerous instances when the main character is trying to name all the facts about Finland that make it an attractive country for Norwegians to visit. Those are often funny and contain that little teasiness the Nordics have for their neighbors, especially for Finland (perhaps the most boring one of them). Other than making fun of their neighbors and Norwegians themselves, Loe is subtly touching topics like loneliness, the sense of feeling at home, immigration and racism.

The book is beautifully written and melodic in some sense. Certain sentences are long and you hold your breath when you're reading but it's worth it, it gives you a certain sense about the thought process in the narrator's head.

Title: Faces in the Crowd
Author: Valeria Luiselli
My Review:
After having read Luiselli's The Story of My Teeth, I was curious to see what her debut novel was like. It was something completely different.

The novel starts out with two storylines - the narrator's life in the past in New York, and her current life in Mexico. But things gradually take a different turn and the line between the past, present and future becomes muddied and the narrators' identities get confused.

The book is magical and imaginative. It's well written and lets the writer's thought process go on paper just as it is, without any censorship.

Valeria Luiselli is definitely one of those contemporary writers whose books I will look forward to.

Author: Liv Strömquist
My Review: Ideologically, this should be something that I should have liked. Feminism, leftist ideas, etc. What's there not to like? However, things were oversimplified here. Bringing in lots of historical problematic men and talking about them was interesting. But I missed the nuance and I missed the historical context.

Title: Resistance: A Songwriter's Story of Hope, Change, and Courage
Author: Tori Amos
My Review:
Tori Amos is one of my favorite musicians of all times. Therefore, I was interested in finding out what she has to say about the current situation in the world.

"Resistance" is the place where the personal and the political meet. Through her personal journey as a songwriter, through dissecting her own songs and putting them in a political and personal context Tori Amos is telling us about the artist's important role of fighting the dark powers.

The reason why I don't give five stars is because I missed a bit of structure and depth into the political.

Title: Little Eyes
Author: Samanta Schweblin
My Review:
Having read Samanta Schweblin's Fever Dream, I was expecting a similar experience from Little Eyes. Whether it was the wrong marketing or my own impressions of Fever Dream, Little Eyes ended up being a completely different experience.

First of all, I have issues with it being called a novel, since the plots of different parts are not interconnected. A short story collection with a common theme? Or maybe just a fictional narrative that doesn't really need classification.

Secondly, I completely disagree with it being classified as horror and/or dystopian. Little Eyes is one of those books that shouldn't be classified and shouldn't be labelled because the labels would be misleading.

Samanta Schweblin's Little Eyes is built around the digital toy kentuki, which connects random people around the world without really connecting them. All the main characters in the book are longing for connection with another human being. Kentukis may give them this opportunity but you don't get to choose who you connect to.

In the COVID-19 lockdown era when we all depend on the internet to stay connected and when we visit each other's homes through cameras all over the world, Little Eyes comes in as a timely piece of literature, taking this kind of communication to the next level - unilateral and with strangers, exploring the dark sides of this connection in a very humane and day-to-day manner.

Little Eyes mostly reminded me of Ray Bradbury's Martian Chronicles - short stories connected around the common theme and exploring human connection.

Title: Writing
Author: Marguerite Duras
My Review:
Writing by Marguerite Duras seems to be about COVID-19 lockdown. It's about loneliness that can equate to madness, about storing food in a storage room during the war and about silence and the unnoticeable sounds that break the silent and break the absolute loneliness.

The book consists of five essays, each one of which focuses on a moment, an emotion, an action or a place that is important to the author. It is written in the typical Duras style with short and tangible sentences. There is lots of white space between the paragraphs and white space is what you really need during a lockdown to read everything paragraph by paragraph.

In the essay "Writing" Duras explores what it means to write, why she write, how she writes, where she wriites and when she writes. Loneliness and writing are intertwined. There is no writing without loneliness and silence. In the essay she also describes the death of a fly. The death of the fly becomes important because it is described and there is someone who had witnessed the death.

In the essay "The Death of the Young British Pilot" the death of the fly is contrasted to the British pilot's death. The pilot has perhaps been one of the last victims of WWII. He had died on the day WWII ended, while his plane crashed in the trees in Vauville, France. Nobody knows the exact time of his death but there is the grave and there is the old man who visits the grave every year and then he doesn't visit it the year after and ever again. The young pilot embodies the war and the ending of the war.

"Roma" consists of a dialogue between two people in a hotel in Rome. The conversation is about Rome, about its existence and importance.

"The Pure Number" consists of thoughts about purity as a word and as a concept. The book ends with "The Painting Exhibition", where another form of creativity is discussed. There is the artist and his paintings and how the paint transforms into a painting on its way from the palate to the canvas. The book starts with writing about writing and it ends with writing about painting.

Title: Babette's Feast and Other Anecdotes of Destiny
Author: Isak Dinesen
My Review:
3.5 stars
Babette's Feast and Other Anecdotes of Destiny is a collection of long short stories (well, at least three of the stories are long enough to be called novellas). A long short story is precisely the length of literary work that is extremely difficult to deliver because usually they feel like too long and lots of details seem redundant. The long stories in this book were no exception. Often it was a struggle going through. However, Karen Blixen is a master of plot. Almost all the stories had excellent ideas and rich plots, which makes them easy to retell to other people.

I can't say I enjoyed the book very much but it was definitely worth the read to get some idea about Karen Blixen's writing style.

Title: Villa Triste
Author: Patrick Modiano
My Review:
Villa triste is yet another typical Patrick Modiano book - characters with a mysterious past and present and with many hints for the reader to figure the mysteries out. Modiano is one of those writers that you know exactly what you'll be getting, if you pick up a random book of his, in a good way.

But Villa triste also has that Hemingway vibe and that Breakfast at Tiffany's vibe. It's all the good stuff in one place with all the melancholy and the sadness. A great read for the quarantine

Title: Women Without Men: A Novel of Modern Iran
Author: Shahrnush Parsipur
My Review:
The reason I picked up this book was because it was marketed as a feminist book, and because I try to read as many non-English language female authors as I can. After having finished "Women Without Men", I have to admit I am quite disappointed.

The book is about five women living in the 50's Iran during the coup and how they liberate themselves from men only to go back to them again.The first part was great. The introduction of the characters and the reality they were in was really captivating. Although the propaganda tone of the book was popping in here and there, it was still a joy to read. The parts about Munes were the especially great ones.

However, as soon as the characters end up in Karadj, the book completely loses its engine. It becomes impossible to understand what motivates the characters' actions. The propaganda is even louder. The dialogues are increasingly artificial. The ending is unconvincing. Yes, each one of the women somewhat get what they want (although through men). But it's not possible to understand how they got there, and why it was not possible in the beginning.

The magic realism is also great in the beginning. I especially loved Munes's resurrections. But as things move to Karadj, it becomes more and more dull and less powerful

My suspicion is that this book became a big hit because of the Western propaganda against Iran ("see how bad things are Iran") and not because it's a true literary masterpiece.

Title: Fever Dream
Author: Samanta Schweblin
My Review: Samanta Schweblin's Fever Dream is the story of dying Amanda a little boy named David who is not related to Amanda in any way. I have to admit that I was so scared when I started reading it that I had to leave it and finish it the next day in broad daylight. Although I'm not a fan of horror in general, I loved this novella. I loved because describing it by the word horror would be too simplistic and the feeling it gave me was not just fear.

Title: Bavian
Author: Naja Marie Aidt
My Review: Depending on what you are looking for in this book, you might either love it or hate it. I was recommended to read Naja Marie Aidt's "Baboon" because I really like Helle Helle's literature. And indeed, the short stories in "Baboon" are written in a similar minimalistic styles. Coming from poetry, Naja Marie Aidt's prose has a certain poetry in them. However, the stories did not reach me at a deeper level. I was desperately looking for some depth or relatability that the stories were lacking. It was usually descriptions of sexual scenes, often quite clichéd (intentionally?) and each story left me with the question "so what?" or "why do I really need to read this?" I do acknowledge though that having read it in Danish I could have missed important details. And I definitely want to go dive deeper into Aidt's poetry.

Title: Naïve. Super
Author: Erlend Loe
My Review:
This book was recommended to me by someone working at a bookstore in Bergen, Norway when I asked for something by a Norwegian author. I thank her for the recommendation. It was an enjoyable read.

The main character of the novel leaves university at the age of twenty-five and tries to find meaning to his life. He is obsessed with time and space, befriends a little boy, exchanges fax messages with a friend and starts dating a young woman.

The book is brilliant in its simplicity and great humour. There is a certain naivety and honesty in the narration that one might find unusual, yet quite charming. Through this character the author seems to be challenging the way the modern world is structured and the demands that are on a modern man. We see a character doing all the things that a grown man shouldn't be doing: leaving university, befriending a kid, playing with a ball and a hammer, crying when watching something emotional on TV, thinking a lot about time and space and valuing the connections he has with other people (instead of money, career, etc.).

One thing that made me especially love the book was the mention of Alanis Morissette and the way the video of Ironic was described. As someone who has grown up listening to Alanis Morissette, I found it important and heart-warming.

Title: Աւերակներուն մէջ
Author: Zabel Yesayan
My Review: The author Zabel Yesayan travels through parts of then Ottoman Empire in the aftermath of the Armenian Genocide and documents the survivors' stories. Despite all the horrors of the genocide that are beyond the imaginable, and the trauma the survivors were carrying, the book ends with a positive note - we still exist. An important read for those who want to know more about the Armenian Genocide.
Tag_Note: Western Armenian writer, born in Constantinople

Title: The Gendered Brain: The New Neuroscience That Shatters the Myth of the Female Brain
Author: Gina Rippon
My Review:
Gina Rippon's "The Gendered Brain" explores centuries old myths and stereotypes about the female brain and the female behaviour. Examining the papers that have addressed sex differences in brain and skills one by one, she points out the shortcomings of such studies and emphasizes that there are more similarities between men and women than differences. Moreover, most of these differences may be a result of living in a gendered society and a gendered world. She further stresses the importance of leaving these desperate attempts at finding differences and focusing on asking the right questions, such as sex differences regarding physiological differences. And quite controversially, she also challenges the views on gender identity.

With sexism being all around, this is an important and empowering book to read. With its scientific approach, the book is providing tools (and literature) to deal with everyday sexism and to have a deeper understanding how the gendered world is shaped around us.

Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
One of the reasons why I don't read Murakami voluntarily is because he himself doesn't know the answers to the questions the reader may ask. Birthday Girl was no exception and I wouldn't have read it, if it wasn't chosen by my book club.
A woman makes a wish on her twentieth birthday and we don't know if it's granted. We don't know what the wish is. Total nonsense. Murakami-style nonsense. And the man earns a lot of money by generating tons of this nonsense. This is not serious literature.

Title: The Parisian
Author: Isabella Hammad
My Review:
With a heavy heart I'm giving three stars to this book because I so much wanted to give 5.

Isabella Hammad's The Parisian follows Palestinian Midhat whose father sends him to France to study (and to avoid WWI) and after which he returns to Palestine. Set in early 20th century, we learn a lot about the history and the struggles of Palestinian people. Blending the personal with history, Hammad provides the reader with valuable information about Palestine that one would not otherwise encounter. Being Armenian myself, I also valued the presence of Armenians in the book and putting the Armenian Genocide in the historical context.

To summarize what the paragraph above, The Parisian is a really important novel and should exist. But it was written in 2019, yet it felt like something from the 19th century, very much Tolstoy War and Peace-like, yet not quite there with its complexity. The text is heavy, often irrelevant and the novel extends to an unnecessary almost 600 pages. I am sure it would benefit from being only half of what it is.

Reading the book was generally a struggle because the side stories were too long, too unimportant and too difficult to go through. What I liked though were the dialogues that were really masterfully written. Furthermore, hidden between the heavy lines of 19th century novel style there were many gems that showed Hammad's great potential as a writer.

The Parisian is a rather ambitious book and hasn't lived up to the ambition as a debut novel. However, Isabella Hammad seems to be a talented writer and I will definitely read her next novel (unless it's about 600 pages again).

Title: 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World
Author: Elif Shafak
My Review:
Ten years after having read "The Bastard of Istanbul", reading Elif Shafak again felt like meeting an old friend many years later. That familiar writing, that familiar tone of voice, the details about scent and taste, the courage of talking about certain topics... It felt like meeting an old, yet matured friend. I was impressed how much Elif Shafak's writing has matured since then.

10 Minutes 38 Seconds is the story of Leila, a prostitute, killed and thrown to the rubbish bin. While her brain is slowly shutting down after her heart stopped beating, she recollects the most important moments of her life. We also encounter her five friends, four of which are right at the edge of the society just like her, and the fifth one is leading a double life. All these people with different ethnic, cultural, linguistic and religious backgrounds and gender identities come together as friends because these things don't matter any more when you're right at the edge of the society.

The first part of the book is just brilliant. The stories are told masterfully, they keep the reader engaged and interested. The characters are vivid. Elif Shafak gives life, a story and a personality to Leila, someone who has been dehumanized by so many. She makes a point by stating that prostitutes have a story worth telling and these stories can be tragic and painful.

I feel a strange comfort when reading female Turkish authors and this one was no exception. Certain ceremonies, traditions, tastes, names and places were all too familiar to me and I didn't need the explanations the way a Western reader would need.

The second part was rather weak but I think the author was trying to do something really brave - to keep the story going while the protagonist was dead. It was quite difficult to keep reading when there was no big engine driving the story. Another weakness of the book were the parts about D\Ali. I think if this character and everything about him was left out, the whole story would benefit from it.

Also, I had an impression that Shafak was using the show-don't-tell technique in a rather innovative way. First she was showing, and if you were an attentive reader, you would notice what she was showing but some pages later she would also tell you what she had shown, in case you had missed.

Altogether, this was a book about suffering, pain and abuse but also beautiful friendships that know of no cultural or religious boundaries.

Title: Efter solen
Author: Jonas Eika
My Review:
Jonas Eika came to my attention only after I had heard his speech while receiving the Nordic Council's Literature Prize. I thought that someone who has something important to say on stage will also have something important to say in his writing. And indeed he did.

"Efter solen", a short story collection set in various parts of the world, is very different from everything I have read before. First of all, Eika is challenging structure. For instance, the story "Bad Mexican Dog" that appears twice in the book, is a story in two parts. But since there is distance (i.e. other stories) between the first and the second parts, one can perceive the first part as a stand-alone story. Moreover, my understanding of the first part was completely different than when the first part was looked at in the context of the second part.

Eika is also exploring sexuality in rather unique way and diminishing the boundaries between the masculine and the feminine. Often it's impossible to tell whether a character is a man or a woman. There are sometimes subtle clues about it. But in general through his writing Eika demonstrates that it's not important.

As a non-native Danish speaker, it was rather challenging for me to read this book and there may have been many details that I have missed. But I will get back to this book again at some point in the future, when my Danish is better.

Title: Deep Mountain Across the Turkish-Armenian Divide
Author: Ece Temelkuran
My Review:
Ece Temelkuran's Deep Mountain is discussing the Armenian genocide and its consequences at a personal, human-to-human level, leaving the politics only in the background. Interviewing people in Armenia and Armenian diaspora in France and the US, she is showing the similarities of individual stories but also the differences among them. What is more striking is that Temelkuran is treated very differently depending where in the world she is.

The book is a succeeded effort of bringing Armenians and Turks together around a table to discuss what they feel about each other but, more importantly, why they feel that way. But the story is unfinished. The book ends with an invitation for each and everyone to start their own journey to get to know the other.

Reading the book as an Armenian, many of my important questions were answered. How do Turks perceive the genocide? Why is it so difficult for them to use the term 'genocide'? What is it like at an individual, not collective level? Many aspects of these answers were eye-opening. Yes, there are Turks who know that the genocide has happened but they feel numb. Why is it so? This numbness is also discussed in the book.

Importantly, it is striking how women are more open for a dialogue and less hostile than men. Women are more eager to tell stories and to connect. And maybe that's where everything should start from - Armenian women talking to Turkish women.

In the end you confirm your prior beliefs - there is the political but there is also the personal. And while there is little you can do at political level, there is a lot that can be done at a personal level. And there I go, it is time for my own journey.

Title: Walking on the Ceiling
Author: Aysegül Savas
My Review:
After an exhausting and stressful week and nobody showing up at a social event I had organized I stopped at a bookstore on my way home. This is how I came across "Walking on the Ceiling". I rarely buy anything without having a bit of an idea what I am buying. And this was one of these rare occasions. I bought the book because of the author's name, because she has lived in Copenhagen and because the brief description on the back of the book was all too familiar.

"Walking on the Ceiling" is the story of a young woman named Nunu. Originally from Istanbul, she moves to Paris after her mother's death to pursue her romantic dream of being a writer in Paris. This is where she befriends M., an author whose novels she had read and loved.

The best books are the relatable ones. And this is one of them. This is not only the story of Nunu but also those of us who have moved to a European city as a young woman, all alone, with nobody to talk to. This is the story of us longing for friendships like the one Nunu had with M. but, unlike Nunu, we never got it. This is the story of a complex mother-daughter relationship that some of us know too well. This is the story of those of us who have left their lives behind, trying to disconnect and distance themselves from their origins and yet it keeps coming back in the form of stories to tell to the people we meet. And this is the story of reconnection and reconciliation with our roots.

But above all "Walking on the Ceiling" is a love letter to Istanbul.

There is also the subtle commentary to the political situation in Turkey, the celebration of Middle Eastern women that are so much looked down on in the West and the typical white man's character who doesn't really get it.

The book is really well written and it also affects the reader at a certain emotional level. It triggers your own memories and your own stories. If you are a young woman who has moved to a big city on her own at some point in her life, this is a must read for you.

Title: Rødby-Puttgarden
Author: Helle Helle
My Review:
In this book the author is showing the life of an ordinary woman and her interaction with her sister, niece, mother and various men. I am amazed by how well the book is written and how much Helle Helle is able to show with using so little language. There is a reason why critics compare her with Hemingway. Indeed, she uses dialogue and minimalistic language to convey many different emotions. However, unlike Hemingway, Helle Helle's characters in this book are not male writers or intellectuals or whatsoever. They are the most ordinary women you meet at the counter of a ferry shop and you think their lives are boring. Helle Helle shows that there are no boring lives.

I wish this book was translated into English.

Title: Jadekatten: En Slægtssaga
Author: Suzanne Brøgger
My Review:
As a non-native Danish speaker, it was quite a challenge reading this book but also the language in the book was so special that a lot of it would have been lost, if translated. The storytelling style was compelling. The most tragic parts were written in a way that you can't help laughing but at the same time you know you shouldn't. The best character work of the book, in my opinion, was Katze with all her ideas, beliefs and philosophy.
Many reviewers mention that the book was confusing with all the characters and their stories but I completely disagree with those opinions. Since the story mainly focused on the female line in three generations (Katze, Li and Zeste), it was quite easy to follow.

It was quite a slow read but worth the time spent on it. The only part that was redundant was Orm's book that we could totally live without.

My Review: It's a pity this book has never been translated to English. While set in a small town in Denmark, describing the lives of ordinary Danes, many people all around the world can relate to the feeling of going back to the place where one grew up and trying to feel home again.
